name: Harlow platinum bleach mixture

card.summary: The ammonia, bleach and soap-flake mixture reported to have created Jean Harlow's 1930s platinum blonde.
card.note: Strong bleaches can severely damage hair and irritate or burn the scalp.

quick.overview:
Jean Harlow's platinum blonde hair made her an icon of the early 1930s. Her hair was naturally ash-blonde, and the shade was reportedly achieved with weekly applications of ammonia, Clorox bleach and Lux soap flakes.

The appeal is a dramatic, near-white blonde that influenced many women to dye their hair to match; the cost was hair weakened and damaged by the process.
quick.how: The reported method was a repeated, home-style bleaching of the hair with household chemicals, maintained weekly. Modern platinum looks are generally done with salon lighteners and conditioning treatments.
quick.risks: Reported effects on Harlow included weakened, damaged hair. Household bleach is a harsh chemical not designed for hair and can burn skin.

lead: Jean Harlow's platinum blonde hair was naturally ash-blonde; the shade was reportedly achieved with weekly applications of ammonia, Clorox bleach and Lux soap flakes, a process that weakened and damaged her hair.[1] She publicly denied that her hair was bleached.[1]

The colour became a sensation. Columbia renamed the film Gallagher to Platinum Blonde to capitalise on the publicity, and Howard Hughes's team ran Platinum Blonde clubs offering $10,000 to any beautician who could match her shade, a prize reported as never claimed.[1]
Her look influenced many women to dye their hair to match, and Camille Paglia credits Harlow with the idea that blondes have more fun. She is also said to have inspired Marilyn Monroe and Madonna.[1]

angle.text: The mixture lightened hair to a platinum shade that became a defining 1930s look, at the cost of weakened hair.

infobox: Ammonia, Clorox bleach, Lux soap flakes

paras: The reported formula combined ammonia, household bleach and soap flakes and was applied weekly to maintain the shade.[1] Harlow denied bleaching her hair publicly.[1]

The Platinum Blonde film title and the bounty offered by Howard Hughes's team helped fix the nickname.[1] Many women copied the colour, and Paglia describes the look as incredibly unnatural and associated with the harlot figure.[1]
